```{r, include = FALSE}
options(width = 100)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
library(AgriDesign)
```

The model of a design is not only a list of terms: each term has to be tested
against the variation of the experimental units to which it was applied. This
vignette shows how AgriDesign handles that in the common designs of
agricultural research.

## Factorials

All combinations of two or more factors, here three tomato varieties by three
fertiliser levels in complete blocks:

```{r}
fit <- design_anova(tomato_factorial, "Yield_kg_plant", c("Variety", "Fertilizer"),
                    block = "Block", transform = "log")
fit
```

With a significant interaction, the main effects are averaged over levels that
behave differently; compare one factor within each level of the other (simple
effects):

```{r}
compare_means(fit, "Fertilizer", by = "Variety")
plot_interaction(fit, "Fertilizer", "Variety")
```

Because the analysis was done on the log scale, the tables also report the
back-transformed means.

## Split-plots and strip-plots

Irrigation systems are hard to apply to small plots, so they go on main plots;
varieties go on sub-plots inside them. The main-plot factor is compared with
the variation among main plots (Error a), the rest with the sub-plot error:

```{r}
sp <- design_anova(split_irrigation, "Yield_t_ha", c("Irrigation", "Variety"),
                   block = "Block", design = "split_rcbd")
sp
```

Compared as if it were a factorial in blocks, the F of irrigation would be
inflated, because the sub-plot error is much smaller than the variation among
main plots. Simple effects use the right error in each direction: Error b for
varieties within an irrigation system, and the pooled error with
Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for irrigation within a variety.

```{r}
compare_means(sp, "Variety", by = "Irrigation")$error$label
compare_means(sp, "Irrigation", by = "Variety")$error
plot(compare_means(sp, "Variety", by = "Irrigation"))
plot_ss_partition(sp)
```

`design = "strip_rcbd"` (three error strata) and `"splitsplit_rcbd"` work in
the same way.

## Latin and Graeco-Latin squares

Two blocking directions, rows and columns:

```{r}
lt <- design_anova(wheat_latin, "Yield_t_ha", "Treatment", row = "Row", col = "Column")
lt$design
plot_field(lt, value = "residuals")
```

A Graeco-Latin square adds a third blocking factor, given as `block`; a
Youden square (an incomplete Latin square) is suggested when the columns do
not hold every treatment.

## Incomplete blocks

When there are more treatments than plots in a block, the blocks are
incomplete. The intra-block analysis adjusts the treatment means for the
blocks:

```{r}
bib <- design_anova(bib_sorghum, "Yield_t_ha", "Hybrid", block = "Block")
bib$design
ls_means(bib, "Hybrid")[, c("Hybrid", "mean", "se")]
```

If the blocks are a random sample of field conditions, the block totals also
carry information on the treatments. `recover_interblock()` estimates the
block and error variances by REML and combines both sources:

```{r}
recover_interblock(bib)
```

Resolvable designs (alpha, lattice) are analysed with two block columns:
replicate and block within replicate (`block = c("Rep", "Block")`).

## Covariates

A covariate measured on every plot (stand count, initial weight) enters with
`covariate =`; the treatment means are then adjusted to its mean:

```{r}
d <- maize_nitrogen
d$Stand <- c(58, 61, 63, 57, 60, 62, 59, 64, 55, 61, 60, 62, 63, 58, 59, 60)
anc <- design_anova(d, "Yield_t_ha", "Nitrogen_kg_ha", block = "Block", covariate = "Stand")
ls_means(anc, "Nitrogen_kg_ha")[, c("Nitrogen_kg_ha", "mean", "se", "raw_mean")]
```
